newsitem.title: GERMANY: Buba takes revaluation fight to the German people.
newsitem.headline: Buba takes revaluation fight to the German people.

text.p: The Bundesbank has taken a fight over revaluing German official reserves directly to the people in a public relations campaign worthy of the best political spin masters in Washington or London.

Central bank watchers said the Bundesbank, in a rare display of unity among the 17 members of its council, had marshalled a slick attack on the Bonn government in terms designed to appeal to ordinary Germans.
"We are seeing a coordinated defence," said Adolf Rosenstock, economist at the Industrial Bank of Japan in Frankfurt. "Appealing to public opinion is the Bundesbank's secret weapon."

At issue is a scheme put forward by Finance Minister Theo Waigel more than two weeks ago to revalue the Bundesbank's gold and currency reserves at higher levels, enabling Bonn to use the resulting proceeds to slash its budgetary deficits.

In an unusual public fight with Bonn, the Bundesbank last week rejected the proposal as an attack on its independence and a move that would threaten the stability of the future European currency, the euro.

David Marsh, Director of European Strategy at Robert Fleming & Co in London and noted Bundesbank watcher, said that appealing to public opinion was one of the central bank's best weapons in dealing with Bonn.
To go ahead with the revaluation, the ruling coalition must win approval from parliament, a task it should be able to accomplish as long as members of parliament vote along party lines.

Over the last several days, however, at least six members of the central bank's policy-making council have hammered home on a theme close to the hearts of ordinary Germans -- their currency must remain stable.

Council member Edgar Meister said on Monday the monetary union project may enter "rougher waters" in the weeks and months ahead and warned that Germany must not lose its role as guardian of monetary stability.

Bundesbank vice president Johann Wilhelm Gaddum, speaking at the same event, further reinforced the Bundesbank's line, saying there had been no change in its position since it released a statement against the revaluation plan last Wednesday.
Even Wendelin Hartmann, who seldom speaks on macro-economic issues, said last Friday in Toronto that Bonn's plans could undermine the euro's credibility.
In many ways, the Bundesbank is preaching to the converted in warning on the euro.
Many Germans would sooner believe the Bundesbank than politicians in Bonn and most polls show a majority of Germans are opposed to giving up their cherished mark.

"I would definitely be more on the Bundesbank's side in this argument. This whole union can only work if the politicians stick to the criteria they have set themselves," said Martin Kueppers, who works for a German car parts company.
Analysts said the Bundesbank's smooth response to Bonn's revaluation plan was a marked contrast to Waigel's efforts to see the scheme through.
The finance minister announced his intention to revalue official reserves on the same day the government learned the 1997 tax estimate was to fall 18 billion marks short of expectations.

Waigel compounded the sense of panic in Bonn by making a last minute appearance at the Bundesbank's council meeting to present his revaluation case, arriving by helicopter from Bonn before a gathering of televison cameras and reporters.
"Waigel was a public relations disaster," Rosenstock said. "It was not well researched or coordinated."

Analysts said that if the Bundesbank is unable to prevent the reserves from being revalued, it will step up its public relations attack, next time targeting financial markets where it could offer complex economic arguments against the euro.
